lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You wake up. The ground is warm. And something is breathing on your face.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Okay. Okay. Nobody move. Especially you, big guy.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Don't worry. He only eats things that run. So, please, don't run.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Sixty-six million years ago, a giant asteroid was heading for Earth. In this world, it missed. And now, you're here.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Wait. You can talk?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Of course I can talk. I'm a troodont. Seventy million years of evolution. You're the one who looks strange.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Where I come from, a rock ten kilometers wide hit Mexico and wiped out the dinosaurs.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Ten kilometers? That's a mountain. What happened?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The impact threw so much soot and dust into the sky that the sun went dark for months. About three quarters of all species on Earth died, including every dinosaur that couldn't fly.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And here's the crazy part. It hit one of the worst possible places, rocks full of oil and sulfur. Scientists calculated that if it had landed almost anywhere else, the dinosaurs might have survived.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: So we were just unlucky?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Very unlucky. A study from twenty seventeen says only about thirteen percent of the planet would have caused a mass extinction.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Some scientists back home even say dinosaurs were already in decline before the asteroid.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Rude. Do I look like I'm in decline?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That idea is still debated. Many dinosaur groups seem to have been doing fine right up to the very end.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Your guide's name is Trood. She leads you through a forest that has never seen a winter.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: It's so hot. Where is all the ice?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Ice? On the poles, there are only forests. And the sea comes much further inland.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: In the age of dinosaurs, the Earth was a greenhouse. No ice caps. Sea levels were around a hundred meters higher than today. In this world, the planet never cooled down so far.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Are those flowers? I thought dinosaurs lived with ferns.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Ferns are for my grandparents. We have flowers, fruit, and grass. They appeared while my ancestors were still around.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And something just bit me. Are there mosquitoes here too?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Of course. Insects are older than all of us. And your blood is new to them. They will love you.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Is that a T. rex? I knew it! I always knew they were real!

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: A what? That's a tyrannosaur, yes, but the one you know died out sixty-six million years ago, even here. Species don't last forever. This is its great-great-great, a million times great, grandchild.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Does it have feathers? Back home, scientists argue about that all the time.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And how hard can it bite?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Hard enough to crush a car. Whatever a car is.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Feathers? Babies do, for warmth. The big ones are mostly scales. Too hot for a fur coat when you weigh as much as an elephant.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Skin fossils of big tyrannosaurs show mostly scales. Their smaller relatives had feathers.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: What is that, in the sky? Is that a plane?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: A pterosaur. When it lands, it's as tall as a giraffe. Its wings are wider than a bus.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And the ground is shaking. Why is the ground shaking?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Long-necks. Two hundred of them. Step behind the tree, please.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Trood takes you to the coast. The sea is warm, shallow, and full of things you have only seen in museums.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Can I swim?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: You can. Once.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Something huge rises out of the water. A mosasaur: a sea lizard longer than a school bus, with a double row of teeth in the roof of its mouth.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Okay, I'll stay on the sand. Are there sharks too?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Sharks are older than both of us. They survived everything.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Smart. Your species learns fast.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Mosasaurs died out with the dinosaurs. Here, they rule the oceans. There are no whales, no dolphins, no seals. Those were all mammals that grew big after the asteroid.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Wait. If dinosaurs are still here, where are the mammals? Where are the people?

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: Down here! Hi! Please don't step on me!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: A mouse?

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: A primate! Well, almost. I eat fruit, I climb trees, and I'm the size of a rat. My family has been doing this for millions of years.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Real fossils of a tiny tree-climber called Purgatorius date to just after the asteroid. Its family probably lived alongside the last dinosaurs. It may be one of your oldest ancestors.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So you're my great-grandparent?

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: Your great-great-great, a few million times great! But here, we never grew up. Every time a mammal gets big, something with teeth eats it.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That's the hard truth. With dinosaurs ruling the land, mammals would probably have stayed small. No apes. No humans. In this world, you shouldn't exist.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Then who built that?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Our nests? My family did. Bigger brain, better hands, and we've had a lot of time.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: In nineteen eighty-two, the paleontologist Dale Russell imagined this exact idea. He took a smart dinosaur called Troodon and asked: what if it kept evolving? He called the result the dinosauroid.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: But yours doesn't look human at all.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Why would I? Your body is good for your history. Mine is good for mine. I keep the tail. It's great for balance.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Many scientists criticized Russell's human-shaped version. A smart dinosaur would more likely look like a big, clever bird.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: So tell me. What did your kind do with your big brains?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: We built cities. We flew to the Moon. We invented pizza. And we also made a pretty big mess.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Hmm. Maybe that asteroid did your planet a favor. Or maybe not.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Trood shows you her town: hundreds of woven nests in the trees, and a field where her family herds duck-billed dinosaurs like cattle.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: You farm dinosaurs?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: You farm birds, don't you? Same thing. These ones give eggs the size of your head.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Okay, that's actually breakfast for a week.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Okay, honest question. Could I survive here?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: For a few days. Maybe. You're slow, you're soft, and you smell delicious.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Thank you. Very helpful.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: The air is fine for you, the fruit is fine. But at night, the small hunters come out, and they hunt in groups.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: That's why we sleep in holes! Want to share my hole?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I don't think I'll fit.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Night falls. Shapes move between the trees. Small, fast, feathered, and very quiet.

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Don't move. Raptors see movement. Breathe slowly.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: Breathe slowly, he says. My heart beats ten times a second!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Trood, what do we do?

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Now? Now we run.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You run. Trood runs faster. Pip rides on your shoulder, screaming the whole way.

lines.speaker: PIP
lines.text: Left! No, right! No, up! Up the tree!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I can't climb that fast!

lines.speaker: TROOD
lines.text: Then grab my tail!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And then you wake up again. A real bed. A real window. Your world.

lines.speaker: CROW
lines.text: Caw. Morning.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Wait. Did you just say morning?

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: It's a crow, not a parrot. And you were talking in your sleep. Something about please don't run?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Long night. Very long night.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: Crows can't talk, but they do something just as impressive. They make tools, remember faces, and plan ahead. And they are dinosaurs.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Dinosaurs? Crows?

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: The asteroid really hit, by the way. The crater is still under Mexico. It's called Chicxulub, and it's about a hundred and eighty kilometers wide.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So in my world, the dinosaurs lost.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: Not all of them. Birds are the dinosaurs that survived the asteroid. In two thousand and eight, scientists compared proteins from a T. rex bone. Its closest living relatives were chickens and ostriches.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: There are about eleven thousand species of birds alive today. And a parrot's brain packs more neurons than a monkey's brain of the same size.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So the dinosaurs never really went extinct.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: Exactly. They just got smaller, grew wings, and learned to sing.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Morning, little dinosaur.

lines.speaker: CROW
lines.text: Caw!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, which world would you rather live in? Theirs, or ours? Tell me in the comments.
